title: Public-domain legal glossary (Bouvier-style)
source: Original restatements of well-known common-law terms for offline use. Not Black's Law Dictionary. Black's remains copyrighted; this file plus FOLIO is the installed workaround.

entries.text: A writ directing a custodian to produce the body of a detained person before a court so the lawfulness of the detention may be examined. It tests custody, not guilt.
The right to be heard in court. In federal cases it requires a concrete and particularized injury, fairly traceable to the defendant, and likely redressable by a favorable decision.

An equitable order directing a party to do or refrain from doing a specified act. Preliminary relief typically requires likelihood of success, irreparable harm, balance of equities, and public interest.
An out-of-court statement offered to prove the truth of the matter asserted. It is generally excluded unless a statute, the evidence rules, or a listed exception provides otherwise.
The power of a court to hear a class of cases (subject matter) and to bind the parties (personal). Without it, a judgment is void.
The proper geographic place for trial within a court system that already has jurisdiction. Venue may be waived; jurisdiction over the subject usually may not.
The party who commences a civil action seeking a remedy. The plaintiff bears the initial burden of stating and proving the claim unless a statute reallocates it.
The party against whom a claim, charge, or petition is brought. In civil cases the defendant may admit, deny, or raise affirmative defenses.
The mental state required for a crime, such as purpose, knowledge, recklessness, or negligence. Strict-liability offenses are the exception.
The prohibited act or omission. Crime ordinarily requires a voluntary act (or legal duty plus omission) joined with the required mental state.
The doctrine that courts follow prior holdings of the same court, and of courts they must obey, on the same point of law, absent a special justification to overrule.
Claim preclusion: a final judgment on the merits bars the parties from relitigating the same claim. Issue preclusion (collateral estoppel) bars relitigation of decided issues.
A discretionary writ by which a higher court elects to review a lower-court decision. The U.S. Supreme Court uses it as the ordinary path to review.
The proposition of law necessary to the court's decision on the facts before it. Dictum is a statement not necessary to that decision and is not binding.
A judicial remark that is not essential to the outcome. It may persuade later courts but does not control them as precedent.
The duty to produce evidence and to persuade. Civil cases usually require proof by a preponderance; criminal conviction requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
A fair probability, based on reasonably trustworthy information, that a crime has been committed or that evidence of crime will be found in the place to be searched.
The constitutional requirement of fair procedures (procedural) and of limits on arbitrary government deprivations of life, liberty, or property (substantive).
The requirement that similarly situated persons be treated alike under the law, subject to the applicable level of scrutiny for the classification at issue.
A bargained-for exchange of legal value that makes a promise enforceable as a contract, as distinct from a bare gift promise.
The failure to use the care a reasonably prudent person would use under like circumstances. The elements are duty, breach, causation, and damages.
A legal-cause limit on liability: the harm must be a reasonably foreseeable result of the breach, not a remote or highly extraordinary consequence.
A defense in certain civil-rights damages actions. Officials are shielded unless they violated a constitutional right that was clearly established at the time.
Judgment without trial when there is no genuine dispute of material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
The pretrial process for exchanging information: disclosures, interrogatories, document requests, depositions, and related tools, limited by relevance, privilege, and proportionality.
A statute fixing the time within which an action must be commenced. Accrual, tolling, and repose rules determine when the clock starts and whether it pauses.
A rule that shields certain communications or information from disclosure or use, such as attorney-client communications or, in some settings, a spousal privilege.
Data stored in electronic form that may be requested in discovery (FRCP 34), including email, databases, logs, and cloud objects in a party's possession, custody, or control.
An instruction to preserve potentially relevant information when litigation or a government inquiry is reasonably anticipated. It suspends ordinary deletion for the scoped custodians and systems.
The destruction or material alteration of evidence that should have been preserved. FRCP 37(e) addresses ESI. Remedies range from curative measures to adverse inferences when intent is shown.

FRE 803(6): a record of a regularly conducted activity may be admitted despite hearsay if it was made near the time from knowledge, kept in the regular course, making it was regular practice, and it is not shown to be untrustworthy.

A report certain financial institutions must file under the Bank Secrecy Act when they know, suspect, or have reason to suspect a transaction involves illicit activity. It is a filing duty, not a public records search.
A prior decision that a later court must follow (binding) or may follow (persuasive) when the later case presents the same legal question.
